newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: No sign of Hitler's Swiss bank accounts, bank says.
newsitem.headline: No sign of Hitler's Swiss bank accounts, bank says.

text.p: Switerland's biggest bank said on Friday it could shed no light on whether Adolf Hitler stashed huge earnings from sales of his political tract "Mein Kampf" into secret Swiss bank accounts.

Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) acknowledged it could not rule out the possibility because it no longer had documents from the time that could back up a newspaper story saying Hitler held numbered accounts at UBS via an infamous Nazi publisher.

Britain's Jewish Chronicle newspaper, citing recently declassified U.S. intelligence reports, reported on Thursday that Hitler held numbered accounts at UBS in Berne that were handled by Max Amman, head of the Nazi publishing empire.
"We looked to see if we had an account for Max Amman, but we could not find one," a UBS spokesman told Reuters.
He pointed out Swiss authorities froze all German accounts in Switzerland after the war. If they found funds had been held by senior Nazis, they turned the money over to the Allies.
"Max Amman was certainly known as a Nazi," the spokesman said, noting his highly public role as Hitler's publisher.
But he said the matter remained clouded in mystery because the bank no longer had records from the time.
"We do not know what happened then. We do not have the records," he said.
Swiss media seized on the story as fodder for a running debate on just how big a role neutral Switzerland played in propping up Hitler's regime and hiding its wealth.

"If the report is confirmed, it will add to the polemics over dubious accounts stashed in Switzerland during and after World War Two," Swiss television commented in its main French-language midday news, which led with the report.
The Chronicle said authors of the 1944 intelligence report cited also believe that the foreign exchange income of Hitler's Nazi party was banked at UBS in Switzerland.

The report follows the recent declassification of other U.S. documents that showed several tonnes of gold seized from Holocaust victims by the Nazis was placed in Swiss bank accounts and divided up among the Allies after World War Two.
Hitler wrote "Mein Kampf" (My Struggle), in which he set out his Nazi political philosophy, while he was in prison for his part in the abortive Munich beer hall putsch of 1923.
Published in 1925, it was made a school textbook after Hitler came to power in 1933 and sold millions of copies in Germany and abroad.
"The discovery of the 'Hitler accounts' is seen as underlining the importance of Switzerland as a banking haven for the Nazis," the Jewish Chronicle said.
The World Jewish Congress believes that billions of dollars belonging to Holocaust victims are still hidden away in Switzerland and it wants the banks to release the money.

Swiss banks themselves have found only around $32 million in accounts that may have been held by Holocaust victims who tried to hide their assets from a brutal Nazi regime bent on exterminating European Jewry along with other minorities.
An independent panel is trying to clear up the matter.
